As expected, the Mild scenario has relatively flatter prices across the day, with the Full tariff showing a distinctive “duck curve” shape. Moving from 2019 to 2030, we see the belly of the duck deepen slightly, and particularly in the 2030 High scenario we see a very substantial range in the average daily price shape, with the average daytime price below $0.15/kWh and the average evening peak price nearing $0.80/kWh (in 2024 dollars). This illustrates how an increasingly renewable, and increasingly expensive, electricity grid can result in dramatic price swings that can enable significant savings from load flexibility. Average daily price shape for an illustrative customer class (SCE large commercial and industrial) across price years, price forecast scenarios and tariff design scenarios There are other aspects of dynamic tariff design being considered by stakeholders and policy makers, e.g. the use of subscriptions and non-volumetric bill components (fixed charges and peak demand charges). This study does not address these aspects of dynamic tariff design directly. The tariff design scenarios in this study are intended to capture the range of load impacts across different designs, as the dispatch behavior of automation technology will largely not be impacted by these non-volumetric bill components. When looking at the presented bill impacts, and effective costs of operating end use devices, it is important to note that our results only represent a fully volumetric retail tariff. Additionally, we assume that these prices will be symmetric and customers with PV or battery systems can export to the grid, such that the presence of these DERs is assumed to not factor into load response behavior. The present study leverages cluster load shapes developed for the Phase 4 California DR Potential Study (Gerke et al. 2024) in order to model widespread impacts of automated response to these dynamic prices. It is important to note that these aggregate load shapes are often very similar across customer clusters, and while the averages our study presents are representative, we may not be capturing the full diversity of potential impacts. This is highlighted in this study by a supplemental EV charging analysis that looks at optimized charging behavior on a driver-by-driver basis, based on simulated driving profiles. v We develop representative price-responsive load dispatch algorithms to cover six end uses across three sectors using two core methodologies, with supplemental optimization analyses for stationary batteries and more detailed EV charging simulations as illustrated in Figure ES-2. Figure ES-2. Overview of end use response models We find very substantial load impacts if we assume every customer shifts load according to variations in dynamic prices. Figure ES-3 shows the aggregate load impact for all end uses modeled on the average day and the day with the peak system net load. EVs have the largest consistent year-round impact (as shown by the average day impacts), increasing daytime loads over 5 GW on average and shedding approximately 1.5 GW of load in all hours of the evening.
